newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German car workers lead sick pay protests.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German car workers lead sick pay protests.

text.p: Germany's powerful IG Metall union on Monday took up the gauntlet thrown down by large employers such as Daimler-Benz by confirming its readiness to strike to keep sick pay benefits threatened by a new law.

IG Metall said the giant vehicle-making group, which is leading a charge by German firms to cut sick pay entitlements, would on Tuesday get a foretaste of possible future disruption with a day of protest involving 60,000 of its employees.

Protests are also scheduled to take place on Tuesday at General Motors' German unit Adam Opel, while similar action is also expected across Ford plants in Germany -- despite the fact that it has not announced its intention to cut sick pay for its workers.

Referring to one of the key events of German industrial history, IG Metall said it was just as prepared to fight for full sick pay entitlements as the workers that secured them with strike action 40 years ago.

"If necessary, IG Metall will choose a strike in exactly the same way as they did in Schleswig-Holstein 40 years ago," Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the IG Metall union representing some 3.5 million metal and electronics workers, told a news briefing.

Zwickel was referring to a 114-day strike by metal workers in the north German state that established many of the working conditions that German workers now take for granted and their employers had -- until now -- learned to live with.

The new law, introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government earlier this month, would reduce sick pay from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent and would save German industry a total 12 billion marks ($7.8 billion) a year.

Vehicle-maker Daimler-Benz last week became the first company to announce that it would be applying the law when it comes into effect this Tuesday without the consultation with workers expected in German industrial relations.
Employees at Daimler-Benz are to retaliate by attempting to bring the industrial giant to near-standstill on Tuesday with a protest day across all the group's activities.
Some 600 delegates from the OeTV white-collar union are due to join workers at Daimler's Mercedes plant in Stuttgart as a gesture of solidarity against the planned cuts.

IG Metall is meanwhile planning a series of other actions across the metal sector over the next six weeks which will include a country-wide day of protest on October 24, the 40th anniversary of the Schleswig-Holstein strikes.
The protests come as other German industrial heavyweights such as Siemens AG and Mannesmann AG have announced their decision to follow Daimler-Benz's lead by implementing the new law immediately.
Other have taken a more cautious approach. Opel said on Monday it would be seeking to implement the new rules in November, and only after having discussed with workers possible compromise measures.
Unions have argued that full sick pay entitlements are included as separate clauses in the majority of employee wage agreements and as such to override them would be a breach of contract.

That argument has appeared to gain ground even within Kohl's government, with Kohl's spokesman on social issues Rainer Eppelmann at the weekend said the employers' decision to go ahead with the cuts was "suicidal if not kamikaze-like".

Kohl himself has said the new measures should be introduced in such a way that existing contracts are not breached, but has not specifically stated whether he believes Daimler-Benz and the others are in breach of contract.

Union including IG Metall have meanwhile stated they are not prepared to wait for a legal determination on the matter which could take years, seeing industrial action as the more direct route to obstruct the measures.
